representations.name: Leslie Lamport
representations.lens: Separate causal order, chosen total order, consensus safety, and the liveness assumptions needed for progress.

primary_sources.title: Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System
primary_sources.evidence_locator: pp. 558-565; sections The Partial Ordering, Logical Clocks, and Ordering the Events Totally.

positions.statement: Happens-before defines a partial causal order, and logical-clock order is not converse proof of causality.
positions.scope: Events connected by local process order and message transmission.

positions.statement: A total event order requires an arbitrary tie-breaker and should not be conflated with physical-time meaning.
positions.scope: Systems choosing a deterministic serialization of otherwise concurrent events.

positions.statement: Paxos separates safety from progress: crash-model safety uses durable acceptor state, while progress needs a distinguished proposer that can communicate with a majority.
positions.scope: Non-Byzantine asynchronous message passing with stable storage after restart.

decision_questions: Which ordering semantics are required: causal, total, or physical time?
Which replica state must survive restart, and what fault model is excluded?
What establishes a stable leader and a reachable quorum for progress?

counterweights.target_or_position: Paxos does not promise Byzantine tolerance or availability for an isolated minority, and state-machine replication requires deterministic execution.

misuse_risks: Treating Lamport timestamps as proof of causality or physical time.
Treating Paxos as an always-available remote procedure call.
representations.evidence_boundary: The selected works support crash/non-Byzantine replication and protocol safety; they do not establish adversarial security or hard real-time correctness.

representations.name: Nancy Lynch
representations.lens: Make failure models, timing assumptions, and the distinction between safety and liveness explicit.

primary_sources.title: Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process
Consensus in the Presence of Partial Synchrony

positions.statement: In the fully asynchronous deterministic crash model, consensus cannot guarantee termination in every admissible execution with one faulty process; this remains distinct from safety.
positions.scope: Fully asynchronous message passing with the paper's admissible-run definition.

positions.statement: A timeout cannot by itself distinguish a failed process from an indefinitely slow process without additional timing or failure-detection assumptions.
positions.scope: Fully asynchronous systems without known relative-speed or delay bounds.

positions.statement: Partial synchrony must state whether bounds exist but are initially unknown or become effective only after an unknown stabilization time.
positions.scope: Consensus protocols with added timing assumptions.

decision_questions: What exact process, message, and failure model applies?
Which requirement is safety, and which is eventual termination?
What stabilizes eventually, and how is that condition measured?

counterweights.target_or_position: Partial synchrony changes the liveness analysis, so the fully asynchronous impossibility is not a claim that practical consensus can never progress.

misuse_risks: Using FLP to dismiss practical consensus systems outright.
Claiming that a timeout proves remote failure.
representations.evidence_boundary: The selected papers establish formal crash-fault and timing models; they are not production SLOs, Byzantine analyses, or generic pessimism heuristics.

representations.name: Eric Brewer
representations.lens: Treat availability as graceful degradation and compatibility-aware recovery behavior during partial failure.

primary_sources.title: CAP Twelve Years Later: How the Rules Have Changed

positions.statement: Partial failure cannot be made transparent by ordinary remote calls; protocols need explicit state, version, and compatibility handling.
positions.scope: Distributed service boundaries subject to partial failure.

positions.statement: Yield and harvest distinguish the fraction of queries answered from the completeness of each result, enabling deliberate graceful degradation.
positions.scope: Systems that can return partial but useful results.

positions.statement: Rolling upgrades require an explicit policy for coexistence, recovery, and handling partitions rather than a static CAP label.
positions.scope: Evolving distributed systems with real partition and recovery paths.

decision_questions: Which requests may return partial, stale, or degraded results?
How is result completeness disclosed to the caller?
Which versions can coexist, and what is the rollback and recovery contract?

counterweights.target_or_position: The selected works provide an architectural degradation lens, not a formal proof of a universal CAP choice or application-invariant correctness rule.

misuse_risks: Using pick-any-two as a design checklist.
Applying one availability or consistency setting to every operation.
representations.evidence_boundary: The selected works address product-facing degradation and compatibility policy; they do not supply a formal consistency theorem or invariant-proof method.

representations.name: Pat Helland
representations.lens: Make autonomous data ownership, message identity, retries, and repartitioning behavior explicit.

primary_sources.title: Data on the Outside versus Data on the Inside
Life beyond Distributed Transactions: an Apostate's Opinion

positions.statement: Autonomous services own code and data, while inter-service communication carries business-level message format and sequencing semantics.
positions.scope: Services defined as independent code-and-data owners.

positions.statement: At-least-once delivery requires durable message identity and idempotent recipient handling rather than a generic end-to-end exactly-once claim.
positions.scope: Message delivery to keyed entities with durable recipient state.

positions.statement: Repartitioning and recovery can cause duplicate and out-of-order messages, so safe handling must be visible to the application.
positions.scope: Scale-out and reconfiguration of entity-addressed message processing.

decision_questions: Who owns the atomic state transition for this effect?
What message identity and deduplication lifetime are required?
Which outcomes need compensation, human review, or irreversible authority?

counterweights.target_or_position: The 2007 argument is an explicitly scaling-oriented opinion that assumes away large-scale distributed transactions and high availability; it is not a universal prohibition on them.

misuse_risks: Declaring all distributed transactions categorically wrong.
Calling a retried workflow exactly once without defining business-effect deduplication.
representations.evidence_boundary: The selected works address autonomous-service and long-running-workflow design; they do not prove a policy for global invariants, liability, or audit.

representations.name: Kenneth Birman
representations.lens: Make group membership, ordering strength, recovery identity, and state transfer part of the system contract.

primary_sources.title: The Process Group Approach to Reliable Distributed Computing
A History of the Virtual Synchrony Replication Model

positions.statement: Membership views and state transfer are part of a virtual-synchrony consistency contract, not merely control-plane implementation details.
positions.scope: Dynamic process groups with common membership views.

positions.statement: Exactly-once delivery claims depend on the stated transport and failure-reporting model; incorrect failure information can produce duplicates.
positions.scope: Fail-stop process-group transport and recovery semantics.

positions.statement: Atomic multicast can align replicas but adds latency, so ordering may be relaxed when concurrent effects are independent or commute.
positions.scope: Replicated group operations with known commutativity properties.

decision_questions: What membership set is authoritative at message commit?
Which operations require total order, and which commute?
How are view change, state transfer, recovery identity, and schema compatibility coupled?

counterweights.target_or_position: The process-group account excludes hard real-time deadlines and persistent data from its main scope and does not establish Byzantine or open-internet semantics.

misuse_risks: Promising end-to-end exactly once across recovery and independent service boundaries.
representations.evidence_boundary: The selected works address trusted, fail-stop group replication and membership; they do not establish adversarial networking, hard real time, or autonomous cross-company workflow semantics.

representations.name: Martin Kleppmann
representations.lens: Require precise CAP terms, latency-aware availability, and explicit offline conflict semantics.

primary_sources.title: A Critique of the CAP Theorem
primary_sources.evidence_locator: sections 1-3; submitted 17 September 2015 and revised 18 September 2015.

primary_sources.title: Local-First Software: You Own Your Data, in spite of the Cloud

positions.statement: Formal CAP availability is eventual response without a latency bound, while operational availability needs an explicit timeout or SLO.
positions.scope: Comparison of formal CAP definitions and operational service behavior.

positions.statement: Consistency and partition tolerance are overloaded terms; a design discussion must state the actual safety property and fault model.
positions.scope: CAP-based reasoning about distributed databases and services.

positions.statement: CRDT convergence can merge concurrent edits, but concurrent writes to the same property can still require application or user conflict resolution.
positions.scope: Local-first collaborative data synchronization.

decision_questions: Which exact consistency, availability, and partition definitions are in use?
What latency is unavailable for the relevant user or workflow?
Who owns conflict resolution when concurrent edits converge structurally but not semantically?

counterweights.target_or_position: The CAP critique is a preprint, and the local-first paper explicitly excludes banking and e-commerce from its target scope; neither supports universal transactional conclusions.

misuse_risks: Saying that CAP is refuted and consistency costs therefore vanish.
Assuming CRDTs preserve every business invariant automatically.
representations.evidence_boundary: The selected works support conceptual and user-data synchronization analysis; they do not prove that critical transactional domains can avoid coordination.

representations.name: Peter Bailis
representations.lens: Test coordination choices against stated application invariants, transaction behavior, and merge semantics.

primary_sources.title: Highly Available Transactions: Virtues and Limitations

positions.statement: I-confluence is defined relative to specified transactions, an invariant, and merge behavior: independently reachable states sharing an ancestor must merge to an invariant-valid state.
positions.scope: The paper's transaction, invariant, and convergence model.

positions.statement: Within that model, coordination-free, convergent, invariant-preserving execution is possible if and only if the transactions are I-confluent.
positions.scope: Globally valid transaction execution under the theorem's assumptions.

positions.statement: Highly available transactions can provide useful atomic semantics but cannot prevent all concurrent-modification anomalies or guarantee recency; some session guarantees require stickiness.
positions.scope: The HAT model and client-session guarantees.

decision_questions: What exact invariant, transaction, and merge behavior must hold?
Can independent commits merge to a valid state without coordination?
Which operations require authority or quorum, and which can use scoped allocation or redesign?

counterweights.target_or_position: The coordination-avoidance theorem cannot establish safety when the real business invariant, transaction set, or merge semantics are incomplete or misstated.

misuse_risks: Equating coordination avoidance with no coordination under any semantics.
Generalizing historical HAT measurements as universal current performance evidence.
representations.evidence_boundary: The selected works provide formal database invariant and merge analysis; they do not substitute for discovering domain rules or justify blanket eventual-consistency approval.
